body: On a Thursday morning a woman of thirty-three is sitting on a low plastic chair in a church hall with a beaker of squash in one hand, because the toddler group is here and it is two pounds and it is warm. Her son is at the far end doing something determined with a plastic tractor. The floor polish smells exactly as it did when she was fifteen, and she notices that the noticeboard by the kitchen hatch still has the same laminated fire notice on it, curled at one corner. A woman she does not know asks whether she is new to the area. She says no, not really, and helps carry the mats back to the cupboard at eleven.

Nobody in that hall knows she had not been through those doors in nine years, or that she looked at the porch for a while before she went in, and nobody is going to find out, because she is not going to mention it and nothing about the morning required her to.

There is an unwritten toll on returning and everybody who has been away knows the amount. You will be asked where you have been. You will be expected to have a narrative — a wandering, a lesson, a tidy arc ending in the present tense — and you will be aware, while delivering it, that it is being assessed.

Which is worth setting against the most famous homecoming in the book, because that story does not work this way at all. The father in that parable runs down the road before the son gets a word out. The speech the son prepared is never actually needed, and the text is careful to tell us he had prepared it, rehearsing the whole way home like a man practising for an interview. He manages the opening line about not being worthy. The rest — the part where he offers to come back as a hired man, having worked out what he thinks he is now worth — is never delivered, because his father is already shouting for somebody to fetch a robe. An elderly man in that culture did not run anywhere, and that is the detail the first hearers would have caught.
This band carries 121 frequencies, of which 46 are playing at this moment. Every one of them starts when you press play, in the middle of whatever it happens to be doing.

Nothing on any of them asks you for an account of yourself first, and that is a deliberate arrangement with a real price attached. A ministry runs on stories: the testimony is how people are moved, how a work is explained to the people funding it, and how anybody knows it is doing any good at all. Deciding not to collect that at the door means giving up the most persuasive thing a ministry owns. It is given up anyway, on the grounds that a toll gate at the entrance is a strange thing for a house that has somebody watching the road from it.

The culture has made this worse without meaning to. Everything now is expected to come with an arc: the fall, the lesson, the return, delivered in the past tense by somebody who has clearly finished the process. There is no format anywhere for a story that is simply shapeless. So the people whose lives actually resemble the shapeless version learn that theirs is not the sort you tell, and they say nothing at all, which looks from the outside a great deal like not wanting to come back.

There is a frequency on this band called The Comeback Room, assigned and in build, and its whole brief is that stretch of road. Restoration teaching for the prodigal and the weary — testimonies and Scripture for people on the long way back, scheduled for the hours when that is when people are actually awake and thinking about it. Nobody is counted through the door of it. Nothing is filed against your name, and no one is going to ring you.
There is an obvious objection to all of this and it is a good one.

It is that the conversation over coffee is not a toll at all — it is a person taking an interest, and being known is a real good that a transmitter cannot supply. That is true, and for a fair number of people the welcome-back conversation is exactly right and exactly what they wanted. The trouble is that it presumes a narrative, and the honest answer is usually not one. Nothing happened. It got hard for a while, and then it got easy not to go, and then a great deal of time passed. That is not a story anyone can tell across a small table while somebody nods encouragingly, so instead of telling it badly, most people simply do not come.
Most people did not leave. They stopped arriving.

A woman of thirty-eight is driving a hire car to her cousin’s wedding on a Saturday, alone, an hour and a half up a road she does not know, having got the car because her own is off the road. She goes through the presets, which are somebody else’s, and gets a song she has not heard since she was in her twenties. She sings all of it. Every word is where she left it, including the second verse, which nobody remembers. Then she parks, checks her face in the mirror for two seconds, and goes in and talks about parking for forty minutes with an uncle, and does not mention it to a single person there, then or since.

She did not decide anything in that car, and there would be nothing to report. Something left in her a long time ago simply turned out to still be working, which is what people mean by coming back far more often than they mean a service or a date.

It would be dishonest not to say what a radio cannot do here. It is not a church. You cannot be baptised by a transmitter, nobody on a frequency will bring you a meal when you are ill or sit with you in a hospital corridor, and a station does not know your name. Sooner or later, if any of this is real, it involves people, and people are the hard part — they always were, and a broadcast is not a substitute for them and should not pretend to be.

But the first mile back has never been the congregation. It is almost always a private business, done badly, on your own, over a period considerably longer than anybody admits afterwards. That is the mile a broadcast is actually built for. There is no door to be seen going through, no first Sunday, nobody clocking your face at the back, and no point in the process where somebody says it is lovely to see you again in a tone that means where have you been. You can do the whole of that mile with nobody watching, which is how most of it has always been done in any case.

So the terms are simple, and they are the ones in the parable rather than the ones at the coffee table. Nobody is owed the story. The speech can stay in your pocket. Whatever you had worked out on the way about what you are now worth and what you might reasonably be taken back as does not have to be said out loud, and would be interrupted anyway.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial and it helps to know they are there. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. You arrive in the middle of all of them, which is the only way anybody arrives at a broadcast.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 309.30 — Gospel Country. There is a practical reason and a better one. The practical reason is that the songs have not moved: country gospel is plain-spoken, built on the old material, and it does not assume you have kept up with what the church has been singing for the last decade, which for a lot of people is the actual barrier and nobody ever names it. The better reason is that this is the format that has always sung about people who went away. It is full of long roads, wasted years and people arriving back later than they said they would, sung without embarrassment by people who plainly know the territory, and none of it asks you where you have been.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. There is an account if you ever want one; it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how the band learns which frequencies people are reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So put HM 309.30 on if you want to, in the car or the kitchen, and turn it off whenever you like. You do not have to tell anybody you did it, and you do not have to have decided anything by the end of it. There is no next step here and nobody is waiting at the other end of this page. The road is quite long enough without a toll gate on it.
